research_concepts: design sensitivity and placebo validation for personnel effects
methodological_questions: Does swapping players in the offensive five shift shot-distance and shot-type mix beyond what game context, clock, and shooter identity explain?
Can a placebo (defensive-five change with offense fixed, or same-offense substitutions that leave shooters unchanged) separate a personnel effect from shooter-level or context confounds?
Are lineup-change windows large enough, per season and in playoffs, to detect a plausible shot-mix shift?
Do derived play-type records or points fields leak outcomes into the shot-mix measure?

historical_evidence.finding: Record reports a PULL_UP exposure slope of -0.0255 with lineup fixed effects and -0.0063 without them; a same-shooter placebo on other play types gave -0.0071 to -0.0075. The record reads this as a shooter-level confound. Its sample and power field is NOT_RECORDED, and its observed_verdict is artifact_found. It is not a lineup or shot-mix study.

Record reports that a within-unit permutation null reproduces a published suppression excess (0.3798 observed vs 0.3744 null, z 0.40), so the excess is described as mechanical under the selection rule. Drift-centering removed the tail asymmetry. Limits recorded: drift, insufficient exposure, selection or regression to the mean. It concerns selecting units on a large drop, not offensive personnel.

Record reports opponent POST_UP then PUTBACK stacking with a stacked effect of -0.071 (n=1,047) against an additive prediction of -0.232. One cluster gradient had an unexpected sign and per-player stacked n was often under 5. Limit recorded: implementation_bug and small_sample. It concerns opponent play sequences, not lineups.

Pilot record on defensive behaviour after the 3-to-4 team-foul penalty, using clock above 2:30 and game x offense x period fixed effects. The penalty contrast (any_fta -0.151) was not distinct from the adjacent-foul placebos (-5.556 and -9.655). Standard errors were not printed. Failure type recorded as E_unclear. It concerns penalty-state adaptation, not lineups.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Exposure-effect estimate for one play type, treated as evidence of defensive adaptation without a same-shooter placebo
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as artifact: the effect shrank from -0.0255 to -0.0063 when lineup fixed effects were removed, and same-shooter placebo play types showed similar declines, consistent with shooter-level confounding.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Published suppression excess compared with matched controls after selecting units on a large drop
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as artifact: a within-unit permutation null reproduced the excess (z 0.40), so the excess was attributed to the mechanical floor of the selection rule; limits were drift, insufficient exposure, and regression to the mean.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Additive stacking of two opponent play types before a star possession
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as inconclusive: the stacked effect (-0.071) was well below the additive prediction (-0.232). The record notes an unexpected cluster gradient sign, small per-player n, and an implementation_bug limit.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Penalty-state behaviour contrast judged against adjacent-foul placebos
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as inconclusive: the target contrast was not distinct from placebo contrasts, standard errors were not printed, and the failure mechanism was recorded as E_unclear.

evidence_establishes: Earlier project studies on related questions (play-type exposure, selection-based suppression, play-sequence stacking, penalty-state behaviour) repeatedly found that apparent effects shrank or disappeared under same-shooter, adjacent, or permutation placebos. Placebo design therefore matters for any personnel-effect claim.
Fixed-effect structure and placebo contrasts materially changed the conclusions in these records, so game, shooter, and context controls are needed in this design.
evidence_does_not_establish: None of the retrieved records studies lineups, offensive-five changes, or shot-mix outcomes, so none directly establishes whether personnel changes move shot mix in this data.
No retrieved record reports sample sizes, power, or detectable effect sizes for lineup-change windows in the 2022-23 to 2024-25 data.
No retrieved record addresses whether shot-distance labels or derived play-type records leak outcomes into a shot-mix measure.
The retrieved records do not show whether the proposed detectability check can return a null result.
own_inferences: The question as posed presupposes its own answer ('showing the design can detect personnel effects'). A positive shot-mix shift is only informative as a detectability check if a placebo that should show no shift also comes out null.
Shot-mix measures built from shot distance and type in raw play-by-play, with no points or made/missed fields, avoid the outcome-derived label leakage seen in derived play-type records.
Lineup changes are not randomly assigned: coaches substitute on fatigue, foul trouble, score, and momentum, so the estimated shift can reflect game state rather than personnel.
Shooter identity is a likely confounder, because the same shooters appear in many lineups; this parallels the shooter-level confound in SF-TMP-009.
uncertainties: Number of qualifying offensive-five changes with enough possessions before and after each change, by season and by playoffs versus regular season, is not known from the records.
The size of shot-mix shift that would be practically meaningful for a personnel effect is not specified.
Whether substitution rotation intervals reliably mark the exact time of lineup changes is not confirmed in the data description.
Whether the derived graph records include shot-distance or shot-type fields independent of points is not confirmed.
Whether the retrieval returned all relevant earlier work is unknown; the results may be incomplete.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved records do not study lineups, so they could not justify proceeding on the grounds that the question has already been answered or shown feasible. They did show a recurring pattern: apparent effects in this project shrank or became artifacts under shooter-level, adjacent-foul, or permutation placebos. That moved the decision from a plain test to a proceed-with-changes design that requires a same-shooter placebo, a no-shift placebo, game and shooter controls, and a pre-specified power check before any estimate is reported.

blocking_constraints.text: Offensive-five changes follow fatigue, foul trouble, and score, so shot-mix shifts can be produced by game state rather than personnel unless game, clock, score, and shooter controls are included.
Without a same-shooter placebo and a no-shift placebo, a detected shift cannot be separated from shooter selection, as in SF-TMP-009.
The sample and power for lineup-change windows are not recorded; playoff windows are likely too small to test a modest shot-mix shift.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved record studies lineup or offensive-five effects on shot mix. The four records concern play-type exposure, selection-based suppression, play-sequence stacking, and penalty-state behaviour. They are cited only for placebo, confounding, and artifact lessons that transfer to this design.

risks.text: Game state (score, clock, foul trouble, fatigue) and shooter identity drive both lineup changes and shot selection.
Substitutions often follow poor stretches of play, so pre-change shot mix may already be shifting (regression to the mean).
Many offensive-five combinations occur few times, especially in playoffs, so per-lineup shot-mix estimates are unstable.
No power calculation is available; a modest shot-mix shift may not be detectable with the available change windows.
A positive result that depends on a single placebo or on shooter-level controls is fragile, as seen in SF-TMP-009.
Several shot-type and shot-distance bins plus several window lengths and season splits create many comparisons.
Derived play-type records include points, so using them to define shot mix could make the measure depend on the outcome.
Shot-distance and shot-type labels in play-by-play may be mis-recorded or missing, which would bias mix shares.
Rule, pace, and three-point usage changed across 2022-23 to 2024-25, so pooled seasons may mix different baselines.
Window alignment between substitution intervals and play-by-play clock could misassign possessions to lineups.

design.estimand: Within-game change in the shot-distance and shot-type mix (share of attempts at rim, short mid-range, long mid-range, and three) attributable to replacing one or more players in the offensive five, compared with the same offense's shot mix in matched windows without a personnel change.
design.unit: Offensive possession that begins within a fixed window (for example, 5 possessions) before or after a single-player change in the offensive five at a stoppage; shot attempts from raw play-by-play are the observed outcomes.
design.sample: Regular-season and playoff games from 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25, using only lineup-change events with at least a pre-specified minimum of possessions on each side; playoff windows analysed separately as a sensitivity check.
design.power: Before any analysis, compute minimum detectable shot-mix shift at 80% power per season and per window length using the actual count of qualifying changes; if the minimum detectable shift is larger than a pre-specified meaningful shift, report the design as underpowered and do not treat a null as evidence of no personnel effect.
design.controls: Game x offense x period fixed effects; clock bins (exclude last 2:30 of periods); score-margin bins; shooter fixed effects or within-shooter comparisons so that shooter selection is not counted as a personnel effect; pre-change trend terms to check for regression to the mean; exclude garbage time.
design.falsification: (a) Same-shooter placebo: shot-mix changes must appear only when the shooter's own lineup changes, not when the shooter stays on the court. (b) No-shift placebo: a defensive-five change with the offensive five held fixed should show no shot-mix shift. (c) Leads: pre-change shot mix should not already differ between windows that will and will not change. Failure of (a) or (b) classifies the result as artifact.
design.multiplicity: Pre-specify one primary outcome (the rim-plus-three share contrast) and one primary window length; treat all other shot bins and windows as secondary with Holm correction.
design.decision_rule: Supported only if the primary effect is distinct from zero with a confidence interval excluding zero, it is larger than the pre-registered minimum meaningful shift, and both placebo contrasts are null. Rejected only if the design meets the power requirement and the primary CI is within the minimum meaningful shift. Otherwise report as uncertain; report as artifact if any placebo is non-null.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25 regular season and playoffs per-game files as available on the decision date (2026-11-02); outcome fields limited to raw shot distance and shot type from play-by-play, excluding points and made/missed fields from derived play-type records.

methodological_questions: Can changing the offensive five detectably shift shot mix in per-game play-by-play data?
What confounders (game context, score, clock, matchup, fatigue) threaten inferring personnel effects from shot mix?
Is the design powered to detect personnel effects given lineup exposure counts across 2022-23 to 2024-25?
Are derived play-type possession records or shot-distance labels a source of outcome-derived label leakage?
args.query: Lineup change effect on offensive shot mix using NBA play-by-play, substitution intervals, and derived play-type records; prior study families on detectability, confounding, and power for lineup personnel effects

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY
